title: Bigger Numbers, Same Four Steps
goal: I can use long division to divide a 3-digit number by a 1-digit number, even when the quotient needs a zero.

card.desc: Practice day for long division. Bailey divides 3-digit numbers by 1-digit numbers with base-ten blocks and on paper, writes a placeholder zero when the divisor does not fit (618 ÷ 6 = 103), and starts with two digits when the first digit is too small (184 ÷ 8 = 23). Seven new words, including placeholder and vigilant.

win: Three digits, one step at a time, and you never omitted a zero!

slides.title: Bigger Numbers, Same Four Steps
slides.text: Yesterday you did long division with 2-digit numbers. Today the numbers have 3 digits. Good news: the steps are exactly the same. You just do them one more time.

notes.do: Set out: base-ten blocks (about 6 flats, 15 rods and 20 units) or play money ($100, $10 and $1 bills), 8 paper plates, whiteboard and marker, paper and pencil, her book. Write Divide · Multiply · Subtract · Bring down on the whiteboard.
notes.say: "You already know every step. Today we just walk a longer road. One step at a time, and I will cheer for every single one."
notes.ask: "How did Show What You Know go last night? Which step felt the trickiest?"

notes.listen: A claim (better or worse) plus an event from the book as proof. If she just retells, ask: "So, better or worse?"

notes.say: "Placeholder, align and insufficient are about today's long division. Omit is the mistake we will catch. Vigilant is how you catch it."
notes.ask: "Why is Stoick called the Vast?" "What happens to 103 if you omit the zero?" (It becomes 13.)
notes.listen: For placeholder: the zero holds a place so the other digits stay put.

slides.title: Hundreds first
slides.text: With 3 digits, start with the hundreds. Estimate first: multiply the divisor by 100, 200…

steps.text: 536 ÷ 4. 536 is 5 hundreds, 3 tens and 6 ones.
Estimate. 4 × 100 = 400 and 4 × 200 = 800. 536 is between them, so the answer is between 100 and 200.
Hands-on. Share 5 hundreds on 4 plates: 1 hundred each, 1 hundred left. Trade it for 10 tens.

slides.tip: The answer to 536 ÷ 4 has 3 digits because 4 fits into the 5 hundreds.

notes.do: Hands-on: 5 flats, 3 rods, 6 units. She shares the flats onto 4 plates and trades the extra flat for 10 rods (now 13 rods).
notes.ask: "How many hundreds can each plate get?" (1.) "What do we do with the one left over?" (Trade it for 10 tens.)
notes.listen: "Hundreds first." She sees the leftover hundred becomes tens, just like the leftover tens became ones yesterday.

slides.title: 536 ÷ 4: the hundreds
slides.text: One step at a time.

steps.text: Divide. How many 4s fit in 5? 1 (4 × 1 = 4; 4 × 2 = 8 is too big). Write 1 above the 5 in the hundreds place.
Multiply. 1 × 4 = 4. Write 4 under the 5.
Subtract. 5 − 4 = 1. Check: 1 is smaller than 4.

notes.do: She says each step and number before you click. She copies each step on her paper.
notes.say: Praise each correct step: "Divide, 1. Yes!" "Multiply, 4. Yes!" "1 left, smaller than 4. Perfect."
notes.ask: "Why does the 1 go above the 5?" (It is 1 hundred.)

slides.title: 536 ÷ 4: the tens
slides.text: Bring down, then the same steps.

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 3 from the tens place. Now you have 13.
Divide. How many 4s fit in 13? 3 (4 × 3 = 12; 4 × 4 = 16 is too big). Write 3 above the 3 in the tens place.
Multiply. 3 × 4 = 12. Write 12 under the 13.
Subtract. 13 − 12 = 1. Check: 1 is smaller than 4.

notes.do: Hands-on: 13 rods onto 4 plates: 3 each, 1 rod left. Trade it for 10 units.
notes.ask: "What does the 13 stand for?" (13 tens: the 1 hundred we traded plus the 3 tens.)

slides.title: 536 ÷ 4: the ones
slides.text: One more round.

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 6 from the ones place. Now you have 16.
Divide. How many 4s fit in 16? 4 (4 × 4 = 16). Write 4 above the 6 in the ones place.
Multiply. 4 × 4 = 16. Write 16 under the 16.
Subtract. 16 − 16 = 0. Check: 0 is smaller than 4. There are no more digits to bring down, so 536 ÷ 4 = 134.

slides.tip: 134 is between 100 and 200, just like the estimate.

notes.do: Hands-on: 16 units onto 4 plates: 4 each. Each plate: 1 flat, 3 rods, 4 units = 134.
notes.say: "You just did a 3-digit long division. Look at your plates: 134 each. The blocks and the numbers agree."
notes.listen: She can say why the check works: quotient × divisor = dividend.

slides.title: 618 ÷ 6: the hundreds
slides.text: Watch closely. Something new happens in the tens place.

steps.text: Divide. How many 6s fit in 6? 1 (6 × 1 = 6). Write 1 above the 6 in the hundreds place.
Multiply. 1 × 6 = 6. Write 6 under the 6.
Subtract. 6 − 6 = 0. Check: 0 is smaller than 6.

notes.do: Hands-on: 6 flats, 1 rod, 8 units. 6 flats onto 6 plates: 1 each, none left.
notes.ask: "Estimate: is the answer about 10, about 100 or about 1,000?" (About 100: 6 × 100 = 600.)

slides.title: 618 ÷ 6: the tens
slides.text: Only 1 ten. Can 6 plates each get a ten?

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 1 from the tens place. The 0 and the 1 make 01, which is just 1.
Divide. How many 6s fit in 1? 0. Write 0 above the 1 in the tens place. Never skip the zero!
Multiply. 0 × 6 = 0. Write 0 under the 1.
Subtract. 1 − 0 = 1. Check: 1 is smaller than 6.

slides.tip: 1 ten is insufficient for 6 plates, so each plate gets 0 tens. Write the 0!

notes.do: Hands-on: she tries to share 1 rod onto 6 plates. She can't. Each plate gets 0 tens. She trades the rod for 10 units (18 units now).
notes.say: "This is the step people skip. You did not skip it. Great job!"
notes.ask: "How many tens does each plate get?" (0.) "So what do we write above the 1?" (0.)
notes.listen: "6 doesn't fit in 1, so I write 0." Point to the word placeholder on the whiteboard.

slides.title: 618 ÷ 6: the ones
slides.text: Bring down the 8. The 1 ten and 8 ones make 18.

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 8 from the ones place. Now you have 18.
Divide. How many 6s fit in 18? 3 (6 × 3 = 18). Write 3 above the 8 in the ones place.
Multiply. 3 × 6 = 18. Write 18 under the 18.
Subtract. 18 − 18 = 0. Check: 0 is smaller than 6. There are no more digits to bring down, so 618 ÷ 6 = 103.
Check: 103 × 6 = 600 + 18 = 618. The 0 kept the 1 in the hundreds place.

notes.do: Hands-on: 18 units onto 6 plates: 3 each. Each plate: 1 flat, 0 rods, 3 units = 103.
notes.ask: "What would happen if you omitted the 0?" (You would get 13, and 13 × 6 = 78, not 618.)
notes.listen: She can explain the 0 is a placeholder: without it, the 1 slides into the tens place.

items.no: Go one step at a time: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.
items.hint: Start with the first digit: how many 4s fit in 4?

items.q: Snotlout found 824 ÷ 8 and got 13. Check: 13 × 8 = 104, not 824. What went wrong?
choices: He skipped the 0 in the tens place. The answer is 103.
He forgot to bring down the 4.
items.why: 8 does not fit in 2 in the tens place, so the 0 is a placeholder: 824 ÷ 8 = 103. Check: 103 × 8 = 824.
no: He did bring down all the digits. The problem is the tens place: 8 does not fit in 2, so a 0 goes there.
Division is the right operation.

notes.do: She does 432 ÷ 4 on paper. Watch the tens step: 3 ÷ 4.
notes.say: When she writes the 0: "Yes! You were vigilant."
notes.ask: On Snotlout's item: "How could the estimate have warned him?" (824 ÷ 8 is about 100, not 13.)

slides.title: 184 ÷ 8: start with two digits
slides.text: 8 does not fit in 1. What now?

steps.text: 8 does not go into 1, so use the first two digits: 18. Divide. How many 8s fit in 18? 2 (8 × 2 = 16; 8 × 3 = 24 is too big). Write 2 above the 8 in the tens place.
Multiply. 2 × 8 = 16. Write 16 under the 18.
Subtract. 18 − 16 = 2. Check: 2 is smaller than 8.

slides.tip: 1 hundred is insufficient for 8 plates. So nothing goes above the 1. Start above the 8.

notes.do: Hands-on: 1 flat, 8 rods, 4 units. 1 flat cannot go onto 8 plates. Trade it for 10 rods: 18 rods. Now share 18 rods: 2 each, 2 left.
notes.say: Praise each step. "You looked first, before you divided. That is a smart, vigilant mathematician."
notes.ask: "How many digits will the answer have?" (2, because 8 does not fit in 1.)

slides.title: 184 ÷ 8: the ones
slides.text: Bring down and finish.

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 4 from the ones place. Now you have 24.
Divide. How many 8s fit in 24? 3 (8 × 3 = 24). Write 3 above the 4 in the ones place.
Multiply. 3 × 8 = 24. Write 24 under the 24.
Subtract. 24 − 24 = 0. Check: 0 is smaller than 8. There are no more digits to bring down, so 184 ÷ 8 = 23.
Check: 23 × 8 = 160 + 24 = 184. The quotient has only 2 digits, and that is correct.

notes.do: Hands-on: 2 rods traded for 20 units, plus 4 = 24 units onto 8 plates: 3 each. Each plate: 2 rods, 3 units = 23.

slides.title: Three things to watch
slides.text: Same four steps. Watch for these three things.

steps.text: Hundreds first. 816 ÷ 8: 8 fits in 8 once. The quotient starts above the 8 and has 3 digits.

First digit too small. In 216 ÷ 9, 9 does not fit in 2, so start with 21. The quotient has only 2 digits: 24.

You bring down right after you subtract, when a digit is still waiting.

sets.q: 636 ÷ 6. What digit goes in the quotient next?
896 ÷ 7. Where does the first digit of the quotient go?
choices: to the left of the whole number
sets.why: 7 fits in 8 (the hundreds), so the quotient starts in the hundreds place: 896 ÷ 7 = 128, 3 digits.
no: 7 fits in 8, so the first digit goes above the 8.
The ones place comes last, not first.
Quotient digits always go above the dividend, lined up by place value.

sets.q: Fishlegs found 424 ÷ 4 and got 16. Check: 16 × 4 = 64, not 424. What went wrong?
choices: He skipped the 0 in the tens place. The answer is 106.
He forgot to bring down the 4.
sets.why: 4 does not fit in 2 in the tens place, so the 0 is a placeholder: 424 ÷ 4 = 106. Check: 106 × 4 = 424.
no: He did bring down all the digits. The problem is the tens place: 4 does not fit in 2, so a 0 goes there.
Division is the right operation.

sets.q: A zero that keeps the other digits in their places is a ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
Which person is being vigilant?
choices: Toothless naps on the warm rocks.
Stoick watches the horizon for enemy ships all night.
sets.why: Vigilant means watching carefully for problems or danger.
no: Napping is not watching.
Forgetting is the opposite of vigilant.
Dropping a book is an accident, not watching carefully.

choices: to the left of the whole number
questions.why: 5 does not fit in 4, so the quotient starts in the tens place: 425 ÷ 5 = 85, 2 digits.

questions.q: Snotlout found 315 ÷ 3 and got 15. Check: 15 × 3 = 45, not 315. What went wrong?

He skipped the 0 in the tens place. The answer is 105.
questions.why: 3 does not fit in 1 in the tens place, so the 0 is a placeholder: 315 ÷ 3 = 105. Check: 105 × 3 = 315.
no: He did bring down all the digits. The problem is the tens place: 3 does not fit in 1, so a 0 goes there.
Division is the right operation.

questions.q: Watching carefully for problems or danger is being ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
questions.no: It starts with v and ends with -ant.

questions.q: Stoick has insufficient wood to fix the boat. What does he need?
questions.why: Insufficient means not enough, so he needs more.
no: Insufficient means he already has too little.
He needs wood. He just does not have enough.
The same amount is not enough.

teacher.objective: Bailey extends long division to 3-digit ÷ 1-digit with no remainder: hundreds first with an estimate (between 100 and 200), a placeholder zero when the divisor does not fit (618 ÷ 6 = 103), and a first digit too small to divide, which gives a 2-digit quotient (184 ÷ 8 = 23). She checks each answer by multiplying.
materials: Class lesson on your laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Base-ten blocks (about 6 flats, 15 rods, 20 units) or play money ($100, $10 and $1 bills)
Whiteboard and marker with the four steps written on it
Paper and a pencil for Bailey
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Packet (2 pages): page 1 on Wednesday, page 2 over the weekend

plan.do: Class slide 1. Blocks, plates, whiteboard. Ask how last night's Show What You Know went.
Class slide 2. What happened since Monday, Hiccup and Toothless (better or worse, with proof), vigilant on Berk.
Class slide 3. 90 ÷ 2 and 70 ÷ 2 on paper; fix any skipped bring-down now.
Class slide 4. Her own sentence for each word; placeholder on the whiteboard.
Class slides 5–8. Estimate between 100 and 200, then blocks and long division side by side, one step per click; praise each step. Check 134 × 4.
Class slide 9. 852 ÷ 6 and 735 ÷ 5 on paper; she leads.
Class slides 10–13. 1 rod cannot go on 6 plates, so 0 tens. Then 432 ÷ 4 and Snotlout's 824 ÷ 8 = 13.
Class slides 14–16. Trade the flat for rods; start with 18. Sort: 2 digits or 3 digits?
Class slide 18. Placeholder, insufficient, align; vast in her own sentence.
Class slide 19. 672 ÷ 4, 721 ÷ 7, 296 ÷ 8 on her own; note which kind she misses.
Class slide 20. Course page: Tuesday night and Wednesday tasks.

watch: Omitting the placeholder zero (618 ÷ 6 = 13). Ask: "Did you estimate? About how big should it be?" Then: "How many tens does each plate get?"
Writing a quotient digit above the first digit when the divisor does not fit (putting 0 or 2 above the 1 in 184 ÷ 8). Ask: "Does 8 fit in 1?" Nothing goes there.
Bringing down two digits at once after a too-small step (in 618 ÷ 6, jumping from 1 straight to 18). Point to the steps: one digit at a time, and every bring-down is followed by a divide.
Digits drifting out of their columns on paper. Have her align each product under the number it came from; graph paper or lined paper turned sideways helps.
Subtraction slips inside the steps (writing 1 instead of 2 for 25 − 23). Have her say each subtraction out loud.
"I can't do it" when she sees 3 digits. Cover all but the first digit with a card: "Just this one. Does 6 fit in 6?" Praise, then uncover the next digit.

packet_key.answer: placeholder → a zero that holds a place; align → to line things up; insufficient → not enough; omit → to leave something out; accurate → correct, with no mistakes; vigilant → watching carefully for danger; vast → very, very large
13 × 4 = 52, not 412. He omitted the placeholder 0 in the tens place. 412 ÷ 4 = 103 (103 × 4 = 412).
Answers vary. Example: 6 does not fit in the 1 ten, so each plate gets 0 tens. The 0 is a placeholder that keeps the 1 in the hundreds place, so the answer is 103, not 13.
308 (3 into 9 three times, 0 left; 3 does not fit in 2, so 0 in the tens place; then 24 ÷ 3 = 8). Check: 308 × 3 = 924
19 (8 does not fit in 1; 15 ÷ 8 = 1 R 7, bring down 2: 72 ÷ 8 = 9). Check: 19 × 8 = 152
210 (the last step is 0 ÷ 4 = 0; the 0 in the ones place must be written). Check: 210 × 4 = 840
Answers vary; uses vast correctly (for example the sea, a huge dragon, or Stoick) with a detail from the book.

teacher.notes: Bailey takes Show What You Know on her own tonight at the end of the After-class lesson. Check her Formspree score before Thursday. If she scores under 90, look at the missed items: if they are placeholder zeros, open Thursday with 618 ÷ 6 and 824 ÷ 8 using blocks; if they are first-digit-too-small, use 184 ÷ 8 and 252 ÷ 7. Then she retakes (a brand-new question set). Page 2 of the Lesson 14 Packet is on Thursday's task list for the weekend.
